title: 2026-12-14 Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching + KV cache cost model
summary: Redwood Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV caching recommendations for Nimbus Fintech's conversational agents. Discussed latency vs cost tradeoffs, expected token savings with KV cache, suggested batching policies and autoscaling knobs for Dedicated, and proposed pilot/benchmark plan. Action items include sending detailed cost model, security docs, and scheduling a pilot benchmark run on customer data sample.

Cost model examples and back-of-envelope calculations
Dedicated vs Hosted for predictable SLOs

transcript:
[Meeting header]
Date: 2026-12-14
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Alvarez (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Nimbus CTO), Liam O'Connor (Nimbus Head of ML), Maya Patel (Nimbus Eng Manager)

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna run through Optimize — batching and KV/prefix cache recommendations and how that maps back to cost. Ethan and I will do the demo and then we can go into pilot details. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Aisha: Hi, this is Aisha, I'm the CTO, got Liam and Maya here.
[00:17] Liam: Hey all.
[00:19] Maya: hi, thanks for having us.
[00:22] Sofia: Great. Quick context from you — what's your primary latency target and are you more sensitive to cost or p99 SLAs?
[00:30] Aisha: p99 is important, we need sub 400ms for user-facing chat and overall cost has to be reasonable; we're migrating some workloads off of our existing in-house stack. curious about dedicated vs hosted for predictability.
[00:45] Ethan: cool — we'll show how batching and KV cache interact. Quick note: some words in the transcript may be off — fireflies sometimes mis-hears "KV cache" as "K V cash" in older exports.

[01:05] Ethan: Alright, demo slide 1: problem statement. Nimbus runs two main flows: short transactional prompts (30-120 tokens) and long context flows for account support (~2k tokens). Stated goals: tighten p99 for short flows and reduce token cost on long flows. Typical concurrency ~120 rps burst to 250 during peak.
[01:40] Maya: correct on the numbers, our current infra struggles with tail latency on peak.

[02:05] Ethan: ok, batching first. Two options: fixed micro-batching (e.g., 8-16) vs dynamic batching where the runtime grows with queue depth until latency SLO. For Nimbus, we demo a mixed policy: dynamic up to batch_size 32, with a max wait of 12ms to avoid large latency spikes. That gives strong throughput and keeps p99 under 400ms in our tests.
[02:45] Liam: is dynamic batching aggressive on GPU utilization? we saw large memory spikes before.
[02:52] Ethan: good question. Redwood runtime uses continuous batching and sequence-length aware packing which reduces waste. We also choose kernels based on seq length distribution — so the memory impact is much lower than naive batching. There will be bumps but autoscaler + burst pool smooths it.

[03:30] Sofia: let's talk KV/prefix cache. For your long support threads, a lot of tokens are repeated prefixes — welcome candidates for prefix cache. Our suggestion: cache the last-turn hidden KV states for common prefixes at the route level and invalidate on doc updates. Hit rate is the key metric.
[03:55] Aisha: what's a realistic hit rate? we have many unique conversations but templated intros.
[04:03] Ethan: depends — for templated flows we've seen 35-60% prefix hit rates; for support threads with lots of repeated system messages and earlier context, 45% is a reasonable conservative estimate. That translates directly to token savings.

[04:30] Ethan: quick back-of-envelope: if average long-flow is 2k tokens and you get 45% cache hit on prefixes equal to ~600 tokens, you save ~270 tokens per request on average. Multiply by your peak rps and cost per token gives large savings.
[04:55] Sofia: we included a simple cost model in the deck — here's an example showing Hosted API cost vs Dedicated with caching. Hosted: $0.018 per 1K tokens (example number), Dedicated with KV cache and batching reduced effective per-token cost by ~3-4x for these long flows in our benchmarks.
[05:18] Liam: those numbers look optimistic, which models were you using?
[05:23] Ethan: these are for the open Llama-like 30B family quantized inference profile we run in the test harness. With optimized kernels and int8 quant, throughput goes up and cost drops. If you use a larger LLM or strict fp16, numbers shift.

[06:00] Maya: how does the cache invalidation work — do we need special bookkeeping?
[06:07] Ethan: Redwood has a cache API and route-level config. You can scope caches to user_id or session and set TTLs. For doc-updates we provide manual invalidation and event hooks for your app to call. For Nimbus use-case, we'd recommend session-scoped KV cache with 24hr TTL and event-driven invalidation when account state changes.

[06:40] Aisha: security — how's encryption for cached KVs? We can't leave anything unencrypted.
[06:48] Ethan: all cached items in Private/Dedicated can be encrypted at rest via customer-managed KMS/HSM. For Hosted we offer encrypted stores with Redwood-managed KMS; Enterprise customers can opt for Bring-Your-Own-KMS. Audit logs show cache hits/misses for compliance.

[07:10] Sofia: a typical objection is warmup cost for caches and memory overhead — any numbers?
[07:17] Ethan: memory overhead is proportional to average prefix length and number of cached entries; in our tests a 1M-entry cache with compressed kvs was ~30GB, but your workload likely needs far less. Warmup will increase initial latency for misses but after hit-rate stabilizes your p99 improves. We recommend a small pilot to measure realistic hit-rate.

[08:05] Ethan: demo time — showing Redwood Console: Optimize tab. (screen share) Here we have workload profiler which shows seq length distribution and potential batching gains. See the predicted batching window where dynamic batching reduces tokens/second cost.
[08:30] Ethan: see the heatmap — most of your requests cluster at 80-200 tokens; that means packing small requests into a pack reduces wasted compute.

[09:05] Maya: can we pin models to avoid fallback to larger models? we saw earlier that fallbacks sometimes increase cost.
[09:12] Sofia: yes, you can pin model versions per route and define fallback policies. For Dedicated you typically pin to a quantized variant. We also support automated rollbacks if quality regresses.

[09:40] Ethan: now the cost model worksheet. (shares spreadsheet) Column A: workload assumptions. Column B: token counts. Column C: hosted baseline costs. Column D: Dedicated w/o cache. Column E: Dedicated w/ KV cache + batching savings. For Nimbus sample trace (we used synthetic proxy), batching alone reduced per-token compute time by ~22% and KV cache added another ~38% effective token saving for long flows.
[10:15] Liam: curious about tail risk — when cache hit-rate drops during incidents do we have graceful degradation?
[10:22] Ethan: yes, Redwood routing supports fallback policies: if Dedicated pool is overwhelmed, route to a lower-cost compatible model or Hosted. You can also enable shedder which rejects requests beyond a configured SLA. We can set circuit breakers per route.

[11:05] Aisha: what about throughput guarantees for Dedicated? our procurement wants SLOs.
[11:12] Sofia: Dedicated comes with commit-based guarantees, autoscaling policies, and optional burst pools. We include latency metrics and per-route dashboards in the Console and SLA addendums in the enterprise contract.

[11:40] Ethan: a quick note on evaluation: our benchmark harness runs your traces in a replay mode, measuring tokens, latencies, and cache hit simulations. For the pilot we ask for 24-48 hours of request logs (anonymized) and we run a baseline vs optimized config.

[12:10] Maya: we may need legal to review logs sharing — what's the minimal dataset you need?
[12:16] Sofia: we only need request/response tokens, timestamps, and route ids; PII should be scrubbed. We can provide a template for anonymization.

[12:40] Ethan: switching to technical details: kernel selection. The runtime chooses optimized kernels based on seq length buckets; this significantly reduces wasted attention computation. For chat models with KV caching, we avoid recomputing prefix attention so per-token cost goes down.

[13:20] Liam: do you have numbers for p99 improvements with prefix cache on long threads?
[13:26] Ethan: from our atlas financial pilot we saw p99 improve from ~1.2s to ~480ms for certain long threads once prefix cache warmed. Your mileage will vary.

[14:00] Aisha: any notable limitations? e.g., multi-tenant cache leakage?
[14:06] Ethan: caches are tenant isolated. For Private installs you control the store. For Hosted we logically shard by customer and provide RBAC and audit logs. There's also an option to disable cross-route sharing.

[14:40] Sofia: let's talk implementation phases for Nimbus: 1) baseline benchmark run, 2) pilot with KV cache enabled for support route, 3) expand to transactional flows with batching rules, 4) commit to Dedicated if the economics work. Does that sequence align with you?
[14:58] Aisha: yes that sounds right.

[15:20] Ethan: demonstration continued — Console shows expected token savings per route if we enable session-scoped KV cache and pack small requests. You can adjust batch max latency slider and see estimated p50/p95/p99.

[16:00] Liam: on the batching parameters, what's the recommended max wait for sub-400ms p99?
[16:07] Ethan: for your 80-200 token distribution, we recommend max_wait 8-12ms and max_batch 32; lower max_wait for very latency sensitive routes.

[16:40] Sofia: pricing nuance: Hosted is simple per-token; Dedicated has infra cost and commit, but with caching you'll amortize infra and drop effective per-token. We'll attach scenarios in the spreadsheet.

[17:10] Maya: if we start pilot, what's the ETA to see measurable savings?
[17:15] Ethan: you should see initial improvements within days for templated prefixes. For broad conversational diversity it may take 1-2 weeks to reach steady-state hit rates.

[17:40] Aisha: security/legal question: do you have SOC2 report and ISO certs?
[17:45] Sofia: yes, we'll send SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 artifacts and our ATO checklist. For Private we support customer-managed KMS.

[18:05] Ethan: small digression: model quantization warnings — for LLMs with strict safety checks or fingerprinting you might want fp16, in which case the per-token cost and cache memory pattern change. We can run both configs in benchmark.

[18:45] Liam: any competitors that do this out-of-the-box? we looked at some things with Anthropic and Replicate.
[18:52] Sofia: Anthropic's managed endpoints are strong for safety but less flexible for custom batching/caching policies; Replicate and open inference projects give control but require more infra ops. Redwood aims to hit the middle: strong runtime plus managed controls.

[19:20] Ethan: going back to the pilot ask — we'll need a grok of your trace and some routing rules. For the first pilot we suggest focusing on the support-route where long contexts yield the most savings. We'll provision a small Dedicated pool and run parallel baseline tests.

[20:00] Maya: cost-ed: is there any hardware guidance? A100 vs H100 vs commodity GPUs?
[20:07] Ethan: H100 gives best throughput but depends on quant/kernels; A100 is common. For quantized int8 we can run well on 80GB A100 or H100; pricing changes accordingly and we'll capture that in the cost spreadsheet.

[20:40] Sofia: let's open Q&A from the team.
[20:45] Liam: how do you handle multi-turn user edits where earlier tokens are changed? invalidation patterns?
[20:50] Ethan: we support partial invalidation — you can invalidate affected session keys and recompute from the closest checkpoint. We also keep versioned cache entries to avoid accidental stale reads.

[21:30] Aisha: any data residency options? EU region requirements for some clients.
[21:36] Sofia: yes, we offer region-bound Dedicated and Private deployments; Hosted can be region pinned for enterprise. We also support private control plane for on-prem installs.

[22:05] Ethan: back to the Console — here's the pilot blueprint template in the resources panel. It lists required artifacts: anonymized traces, target SLOs, route config, and acceptance criteria. We'll pre-fill this for Nimbus.

[22:35] Maya: quick nit — latency numbers in the UI show p50/p95/p99; can we export to CSV for our BI?
[22:40] Ethan: yes, you can export raw traces and per-token metrics.

[23:00] Sofia: we're approaching the last 30 minutes. Let's do a recap and next steps. Ethan, do you want to lead?
[23:06] Ethan: sure. Recap: 1) run baseline replay of 24-48 hrs traces, 2) enable session-scoped KV cache for the support route in pilot, 3) tune batching policy (dynamic up to 32, max_wait 8-12ms), 4) run benchmark and review cost model, 5) if economics check out, migrate transactional flows and consider Dedicated commit.

[23:40] Aisha: good. Timeline?
[23:43] Sofia: we'll send the cost model + pilot proposal by Thu 12/16, and we suggest kickoff 12/21.

[24:00] Liam: legal will need the SOC2 and DPA too.
[24:05] Sofia: noted — sending SOC2/ISO and DPA today.

[24:20] Maya: any final technical caveats we should be aware of?
[24:24] Ethan: warmup and cold-cache tail risk; model quantization can change generation quality slightly — we'll surface any quality regression in the eval harness.

[25:00] Sofia: ok, thanks all. We'll follow up with the spreadsheet and pilot runbook. Anything else from Nimbus side?
[25:10] Aisha: no, thanks, excited to see the pilot.
[25:15] Sofia: great — we'll wrap.

[25:20] (meeting continues with some side Qs and clarifications; last 27 minutes were mostly go-deep on technical knobs and contract questions; truncated here)

[40:00] Ethan: quick follow-up on a technical point — for sequence packing we prefer left-aligned packing for chat to preserve role markers; some open-source packers do right-aligned which confuses role tokens.
[41:10] Liam: noted.

[42:00] Sofia: on pricing, small correction — the Hosted per-1K token number I quoted is example only; official pricing will be in the spreadsheet.

[44:30] Ethan: we also flagged a potential 10-15% additional savings if you cache frequently used embeddings for reranking in the support flow, though that adds complexity.

[46:00] Maya: ok, will review the spreadsheet and get back with dates.

[48:15] Sofia: final recap of owners: Sofia will send cost model + security docs; Ethan will share benchmark runbook; Liam will provide traces.

[52:00] Sofia: thanks everyone, bye.
notes: Transcript intentionally retains natural speech patterns, occasional filler words, and minor transcription artifacts. References to pricing numbers are illustrative; official pricing to be provided in follow-up.
